# Simulating lines, pools and crosses {#sec-simulating-crosses} The Foundations part defined the quantities the book manages -- coancestry (@sec-coancestry) and its partition over two pools (@sec-subdivided) -- and the response they are traded against (@sec-response). @sec-response drew its data from `simulate_pools()` without deriving it. This chapter builds the generator step by step, with `simulate_lines()` and `simulate_data()`. `simulate_pools()` uses the same Balding-Nichols pool frequencies, homozygous lines and A x B factorial, but a different trait: `n_qtl` loci with independent effects plus noise, where the traits built here have correlated effects at every marker and no noise. Up to the lines the two generators consume R's random stream in the same order, so with the arguments of @sec-response (25 + 25 lines, $m$ = 2000, `fst` = 0.15, seed 1) they return the same lines and the same hybrid marker matrix `X` (asserted below); only the traits differ. Everything downstream of this chapter consumes three objects and knows nothing about where they came from. That is deliberate: it is the seam at which a simulation is swapped for real data, and it is the only place that has to change when it is. This chapter builds those objects. It also builds the candidate pool the rest of the book selects from, so the choices made here -- how divergent the pools are, how the index is constructed -- determine what the later chapters have to work with. ## What has to be produced @tbl-stage1-contract lists the three objects, and the optional fourth. ::: {#tbl-stage1-contract .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='The stage-1 contract: the objects stage 1 hands to stage 2, with their shape (N hybrids, m markers, L lines) and the computations that need them. Stage 2 runs without `fL`; it loses only the pool decomposition.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Object |Shape |Content |Needed for | |:---------|:------------------|:-------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------| |`X` |N x m |hybrid marker matrix, values in 0/0.5/1 |every frequency-based metric | |`f` |N x N |molecular coancestry of the hybrids |every coancestry-based metric | |`hybrids` |N x (3 + n_traits) |hybrid id, the two parent lines, predicted traits |the index, and the line-usage vector | |`fL` |L x L, optional |coancestry BETWEEN LINES |only the heterotic-group decomposition | ::: ::: ## Simulating the lines Two heterotic pools are generated with the Balding-Nichols model [@balding1995]. Ancestral allele frequencies $p^{*}_k$ are drawn uniform on $[0.05, 0.95]$, then pool A's frequency at marker $k$ is drawn as $$p_{Ak} \sim \text{Beta}\!\left(p^{*}_k \frac{1 - F_{BN}}{F_{BN}},\; (1 - p^{*}_k) \frac{1 - F_{BN}}{F_{BN}}\right),$$ {#eq-balding-nichols} and independently for pool B ($p_{Bk}$), where $k = 1, \dots, m$ indexes markers, $p^{*}_k \in [0.05, 0.95]$ is the ancestral frequency of the allele coded 1, $p_{Ak}, p_{Bk} \in (0, 1)$ are the pool frequencies of that allele, and $F_{BN} \in (0, 1)$ is the parameter `fst` of the configuration (@sec-notation). The Beta of @eq-balding-nichols has mean $p^{*}_k$ and variance $F_{BN}\, p^{*}_k (1 - p^{*}_k)$: $F_{BN}$ is the expected divergence of *each* pool from the ancestral frequency, not between the two pools. Between them, $\mathrm{Var}(p_{Ak} - p_{Bk}) = 2 F_{BN}\, p^{*}_k (1 - p^{*}_k)$, and the $F_{ST}$ statistic of @eq-f-stats computed on two pools of unbounded size estimates approximately $F_{BN}/(2 - F_{BN})$ (@sec-notation): at the book's $F_{BN}$ = 0.15 that is 0.081, not 0.15. Genotypes are then drawn as $2 \times \text{Bernoulli}(p)$, which makes every line fully homozygous, as an inbred line should be. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} simulate_lines #> function (cfg) #> { #> set.seed(cfg$seed) #> p_anc <- stats::runif(cfg$m, 0.05, 0.95) #> bn <- function(p, fst) { #> stats::rbeta(length(p), p * (1 - fst)/fst, (1 - p) * #> (1 - fst)/fst) #> } #> pA <- bn(p_anc, cfg$fst) #> pB <- bn(p_anc, cfg$fst) #> draw <- function(n, p) { #> matrix(2L * stats::rbinom(n * length(p), 1, rep(p, each = n)), #> nrow = n) #> } #> L <- rbind(draw(cfg$n_pool_A, pA), draw(cfg$n_pool_B, pB)) #> storage.mode(L) <- "double" #> L #> } #> #> ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} L <- simulate_lines(book_cfg) stopifnot(all(L %in% c(0, 2))) # same lines and X as the simulate_pools() call of @sec-response sim_02b <- simulate_pools(n_A = book_cfg$n_pool_A, n_B = book_cfg$n_pool_B, m = book_cfg$m, fst = 0.15, seed = 1) stopifnot(identical(2 * sim_02b[["GL"]], L), identical(sim_02b[["X"]], simulate_data(book_cfg)[["X"]])) dim(L) #> [1] 50 2000 table(as.vector(L[1:5, 1:200])) #> #> 0 2 #> 480 520 ``` ::: Only 0 and 2 appear: no residual heterozygotes. With real data those must be imputed or dropped before this point, because the hybrid-genotype identity in @sec-coancestry assumes homozygous parents. ### The divergence knob `fst` is the single most consequential parameter in the simulation, because it sets how much of the pools' diversity sits *between* them rather than within. What that buys is less obvious than it looks: @fig-divergence-het plots the heterozygous fraction of the F1 over a grid of $F_{BN}$, @tbl-divergence-grid gives the coancestries and diversity components behind it, and @tbl-divergence-trade the changes between the two ends of the grid. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fst_grid <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25, 0.40) div <- vapply(fst_grid, function(fst) { cfg <- modifyList(book_cfg, list(fst = fst, m = 1500)) Lx <- simulate_lines(cfg) fL <- molecular_coancestry(Lx / 2) A <- seq_len(cfg$n_pool_A); B <- cfg$n_pool_A + seq_len(cfg$n_pool_B) f_til <- mean(c(fL[A, A], fL[B, B])) # group coancestry, self included f_bar <- mean(fL) # a hybrid A x B is heterozygous wherever its parents differ c(between_pool_f = mean(fL[A, B]), within_pool_f = f_til, het_fraction = 1 - mean(fL[A, B]), GD_WS = 1 - f_til, GD_BS = f_til - f_bar, GD_T = 1 - f_bar) }, numeric(6)) d <- data.frame(fst = fst_grid, t(div)) # equal pool sizes: 1 - f_AB = GD_T + GD_BS exactly stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(d$het_fraction, d$GD_T + d$GD_BS))) het_exp <- 2 * (0.5 - (0.9^2 / 12 + 0.25)) # 2 E[p(1-p)], p ~ U(0.05, 0.95) plot(d$fst, d$het_fraction, type = "b", pch = 19, ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = expression(F[BN]), ylab = "heterozygous fraction of the F1") abline(h = het_exp, lty = 2) grid() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Heterozygous fraction of the A x B F1 (fraction of markers at which the two inbred parent lines differ, averaged over every A x B hybrid) against the Balding-Nichols parameter, one simulated pair of pools per point at the book scale with m = 1500 markers, the same ancestral frequencies at every point. Dashed line: its expectation, 2 E[p*(1 - p*)] for p* uniform on [0.05, 0.95], which does not depend on the parameter.](03-simulating-crosses_files/figure-html/fig-divergence-het-1.png){#fig-divergence-het fig-align='center' fig-alt='Line plot of the heterozygous fraction of the F1, on a 0 to 1 axis, against the Balding-Nichols parameter from 0.02 to 0.40; the points stay flat along a dashed horizontal line at the expectation' width=1050} ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-divergence-grid .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Divergence grid behind @fig-divergence-het, one simulated pair of pools per row (book scale, m = 1500 markers). `fst`: the Balding-Nichols parameter $F_{BN}$; `between_pool_f`: mean line coancestry between pools; `within_pool_f`: group coancestry within a pool, self-coancestry included ($\tilde f$); `het_fraction`: heterozygous fraction of the A x B F1; `GD_WS`, `GD_BS`, `GD_T`: the gene-diversity components of @sec-subdivided.'} ```{.r .cell-code} fmt(d) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| fst| between_pool_f| within_pool_f| het_fraction| GD_WS| GD_BS| GD_T| |----:|--------------:|-------------:|------------:|------:|------:|------:| | 0.02| 0.6349| 0.6564| 0.3651| 0.3436| 0.0107| 0.3543| | 0.05| 0.6362| 0.6684| 0.3638| 0.3316| 0.0161| 0.3477| | 0.10| 0.6364| 0.6877| 0.3636| 0.3123| 0.0256| 0.3380| | 0.15| 0.6326| 0.7052| 0.3674| 0.2948| 0.0363| 0.3311| | 0.25| 0.6370| 0.7387| 0.3630| 0.2613| 0.0509| 0.3122| | 0.40| 0.6274| 0.7898| 0.3726| 0.2102| 0.0812| 0.2914|
::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} n_g <- nrow(d) dWS <- d$GD_WS[n_g] - d$GD_WS[1] dBS <- d$GD_BS[n_g] - d$GD_BS[1] dT <- d$GD_T[n_g] - d$GD_T[1] ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # the two trade ratios over replicate grids; simulate_lines() seeds from cfg$seed gd_ends <- function(fst, seed) { cfg <- modifyList(book_cfg, list(fst = fst, m = 1500, seed = seed)) fL <- molecular_coancestry(simulate_lines(cfg) / 2) A <- seq_len(cfg$n_pool_A); B <- cfg$n_pool_A + seq_len(cfg$n_pool_B) f_til <- mean(c(fL[A, A], fL[B, B])); f_bar <- mean(fL) c(GD_WS = 1 - f_til, GD_BS = f_til - f_bar, GD_T = 1 - f_bar) } n_rep <- 200 rep_ratio <- vapply(seq_len(n_rep), function(s) { x <- gd_ends(max(fst_grid), s) - gd_ends(min(fst_grid), s) c(-x[["GD_BS"]] / x[["GD_T"]], -x[["GD_WS"]] / x[["GD_BS"]]) }, numeric(2)) ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-divergence-trade .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Change in each gene-diversity component of @tbl-divergence-grid from the smallest to the largest $F_{BN}$ of the grid (largest minus smallest), and the two ratios between those changes. Same single draw per grid point as @tbl-divergence-grid.'} ```{.r .cell-code} fmt(data.frame( quantity = c("change in GD_WS", "change in GD_BS", "change in GD_T", "GD_BS gain / GD_T loss", "GD_WS loss / GD_BS gain"), value = c(dWS, dBS, dT, -dBS / dT, -dWS / dBS))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|quantity | value| |:-----------------------|-------:| |change in GD_WS | -0.1334| |change in GD_BS | 0.0705| |change in GD_T | -0.0629| |GD_BS gain / GD_T loss | 1.1201| |GD_WS loss / GD_BS gain | 1.8928|
::: ::: Across a 20-fold range of $F_{BN}$ the heterozygous fraction stays between 0.363 and 0.3726, against an expectation of 0.365 that contains no $F_{BN}$. Each point is one draw of a finite pair of pools, and the spread over replicate draws was not measured here. Over the same range, in the terms of @sec-subdivided with $\tilde f$ the group coancestry within a pool (self-coancestry included, `within_pool_f`), the within-subpopulation gene diversity $GD_{WS} = 1 - \tilde f = GD_{WI} + GD_{BI}$ of @eq-gd-partition changes by -0.1334, $GD_{BS}$ by 0.0705 and $GD_T$ by -0.0629. The $GD_{BS}$ gain is 1.12 times the $GD_T$ loss and the within-pool loss is 1.89 times the $GD_{BS}$ gain; the expectations under drift in two equal pools are 1 and 2 (@sec-subdivided). Both ratios are single draws. Over 200 replicate grids (seeds 1 to 200, the two ends of the grid only) they have mean 1.002 and 2.008 with standard deviation 0.104 and 0.102, so the departure of this draw from 1 and 2 is within ordinary sampling variation. The `stopifnot()` in the code of @fig-divergence-het asserts the identity that ties the first trade to the flat line: with equal pool sizes the heterozygous fraction is exactly $GD_T + GD_{BS}$, so a constant heterozygous fraction means that what $GD_{BS}$ gains, $GD_T$ loses. That is not an artefact of this grid. The heterozygous fraction of an A x B hybrid of inbred parents is exactly `1 - theta_AB`, and @sec-heterosis-flat derives the expectations for pools of unbounded size: the shared term $2\bar p(1 - \bar p)$, which is $GD_T$ here, loses $F_{BN}\,p^{*}(1-p^{*})$ and the divergence term, which is $GD_{BS}$, gains the same amount. Here $GD_T$ and $GD_{BS}$ are computed from the sample frequencies of $n$ lines per pool, which add binomial variance $p_{Ak}(1 - p_{Ak})/n$ to each pool frequency; then $E[GD_{BS}] = F_{BN}\,p^{*}q^{*} + (1 - F_{BN})\,p^{*}q^{*}/n$ per marker, with $q^{*} = 1 - p^{*}$, and the loss of $GD_T$ and the gain of $GD_{BS}$ are both $F_{BN}\,p^{*}q^{*}(1 - 1/n)$ in expectation. The factor $(1 - 1/n)$ cancels in the ratios 1 and 2. With $n$ = 25 and the $F_{BN}$ range of the grid, the expected change is 0.0666, against 0.0693 for unbounded pools. Neutral divergence relocates diversity; it does not create heterosis. @tbl-keystone in @sec-subdivided states that `GD_BS` is nonetheless to be preserved rather than minimised, and defers the argument to @sec-heterosis; @sec-heterosis-alignment is what has to be true of the divergence for it to be worth anything. ## From lines to hybrids Every A x B combination is formed. With 25 lines per pool that is 625 candidates; at the production scale of 71 lines per pool it is 5041. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} cfg <- book_cfg a_ids <- seq_len(cfg$n_pool_A) b_ids <- cfg$n_pool_A + seq_len(cfg$n_pool_B) ped <- expand.grid(a = a_ids, b = b_ids) M <- (L[ped$a, , drop = FALSE] + L[ped$b, , drop = FALSE]) / 2 # 0/1/2 dim(M) #> [1] 625 2000 head(ped, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| a| b| |--:|--:| | 1| 26| | 2| 26| | 3| 26|
::: ::: The factorial structure matters more than it looks. Because every line appears in many candidate hybrids, selecting hybrids is really selecting *line usage* -- and that observation, made precise in @sec-collapse, is what makes the whole problem tractable at production scale. ## Predicted traits Marker effects are drawn correlated across traits, through a Cholesky factor of a fixed correlation matrix, and the predicted values are the centered marker matrix times those effects: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(cfg$seed + 99) R <- matrix(c(1, 0.3, -0.3, 0.3, 1, 0.1, -0.3, 0.1, 1), 3, 3) vr <- vanraden_G(M) B <- matrix(rnorm(cfg$m * cfg$n_traits), cfg$m) %*% chol(R) traits <- scale(vr$Z %*% B) rank_Z <- qr(vr$Z)$rank stopifnot(rank_Z == cfg$n_pool_A + cfg$n_pool_B - 2) ``` ::: @tbl-trait-cor sets the realised correlations of the predicted traits beside the target `R`. ::: {#tbl-trait-cor .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Target correlation `R` of the marker effects and realised correlation of the predicted traits over the hybrids, for each pair of traits; one draw of marker effects at the book scale.'} ```{.r .cell-code} ij <- which(upper.tri(R), arr.ind = TRUE) fmt(data.frame(traits = paste(ij[, 1], "x", ij[, 2]), target_R = R[ij], realised = cor(traits)[ij]), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|traits | target_R| realised| |:------|--------:|--------:| |1 x 2 | 0.3| 0.259| |1 x 3 | -0.3| -0.440| |2 x 3 | 0.1| 0.049|
::: ::: The Cholesky step gives each row of `B`, the effects of one marker on the 3 traits, covariance `R`. It does not make the realised trait correlations equal `R`: they depart from it by up to 0.14 in absolute value. The hybrid values are linear combinations of the columns of the centred matrix `Z`, whose rank is 48 $= (n_A - 1) + (n_B - 1)$ for an additive A x B factorial, so each realised correlation rests on one draw of effects projected onto 48 dimensions. The target is a property of the effect distribution, not of this draw; how closely the realised correlations approach it on average over draws was not measured here. ::: {.callout-important} ## What this simulation deliberately does not model These predicted values are constructed from *known* marker effects, so they carry no prediction error. Real genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs) do. The book therefore treats `ctx$index` as given throughout, and the reader should read every gain figure as an upper bound on what a real programme would realise. The additive model also carries no dominance, so it cannot express specific combining ability -- see the caveats in @sec-case-study. ::: ## The two matrices, both built ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} X <- M / 2 ctx <- build_ctx(X = X, f = molecular_coancestry(X), G = vr$G, traits = traits, ped = ped, n_lines = nrow(L), pool = rep(c("A", "B"), c(cfg$n_pool_A, cfg$n_pool_B)), fL = molecular_coancestry(L / 2), cfg = cfg) # the heterozygous fraction of hybrid (a, b) is 1 - fL[a, b] (inbred parents) stopifnot(abs(sum(ctx[["G"]])) < 1e-8, min(ctx[["f"]]) >= 0, max(ctx[["f"]]) <= 1, isTRUE(all.equal(ctx[["f"]], tcrossprod(cbind(X, 1 - X)) / ncol(X))), isTRUE(all.equal(rowMeans(ctx[["X"]] == 0.5), 1 - ctx[["fL"]][cbind(ped$a, ped$b)]))) ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-ctx-check .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Size of the context built above (N hybrids, m markers, number of lines) and the two properties checked on its matrices: the sum of the elements of VanRaden\'s G and the range of the molecular coancestry f. Values rounded to 4 decimals; the code asserts |sum(G)| < 1e-8.'} ```{.r .cell-code} fmt(data.frame( quantity = c("N", "m", "n_lines", "sum(G)", "min(f)", "max(f)"), value = c(ctx[["N"]], ctx[["m"]], ctx[["n_lines"]], sum(ctx[["G"]]), min(ctx[["f"]]), max(ctx[["f"]])))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|quantity | value| |:--------|---------:| |N | 625.0000| |m | 2000.0000| |n_lines | 50.0000| |sum(G) | 0.0000| |min(f) | 0.6448| |max(f) | 0.8318|
::: ::: @tbl-ctx-check shows the result: `sum(G)` is zero to machine precision, as it must be for VanRaden's centred matrix [@vanraden2008], and `f` is inside $[0, 1]$: the two properties from @sec-coancestry, on this dataset. The context also freezes two things that must never be recomputed per scenario: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} str(ctx[c("p0", "maf_pop", "index")], max.level = 1) #> List of 3 #> $ p0 : num [1:2000] 0.44 0.3 0.56 0.9 0.12 0.98 0.98 0.7 0.64 0.22 ... #> $ maf_pop: num [1:2000] 0.44 0.3 0.44 0.1 0.12 0.02 0.02 0.3 0.36 0.22 ... #> $ index : num [1:625] -0.291 0.498 -0.361 -0.186 -0.348 ... ``` ::: `p0` is the candidate-pool allele frequency vector. It is the **base** against which `F_hom` and `F_drift` are measured in @sec-genomic-era, and recomputing it per scenario would silently zero out the historical memory of erosion. ## The stage-1 contract in one call All of the above is `simulate_data()`, which builds the same `ctx` as this chapter. `stage1_simulate()` passes its `X`, `ped`, `traits` and `fL` to `stage1_build()`, the function real data enter through: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} stage1_build #> function (X, ped, traits, fL = NULL, coding = NULL) #> { #> if (is.null(coding)) { #> if (max(X, na.rm = TRUE) > 1) { #> coding <- "012" #> } #> else { #> if (all(X[!is.na(X)] %in% c(0, 1))) #> warning("X holds only 0 and 1: ambiguous coding, read as 0/0.5/1 ", #> "(inbred lines). Pass coding = \"012\" if these are dosages ", #> "with no dosage-2 call.", call. = FALSE) #> coding <- "0-0.5-1" #> } #> } #> coding <- match.arg(coding, c("012", "0-0.5-1")) #> if (coding == "012") #> X <- X/2 #> stopifnot(min(X, na.rm = TRUE) >= 0, max(X, na.rm = TRUE) <= #> 1, nrow(X) == nrow(ped), nrow(X) == nrow(traits)) #> hybrids <- data.frame(hybrid = seq_len(nrow(X)), line_A = as.integer(ped$a), #> line_B = as.integer(ped$b), traits) #> list(X = X, f = molecular_coancestry(X), hybrids = hybrids, #> fL = fL) #> } #> #> ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} st1 <- stage1_simulate(book_cfg) str(st1, max.level = 1) #> List of 4 #> $ X : num [1:625, 1:2000] 0.5 0.5 0 0 0 0.5 0.5 0 0 0 ... #> $ f : num [1:625, 1:625] 0.818 0.74 0.743 0.738 0.745 ... #> $ hybrids:'data.frame': 625 obs. of 6 variables: #> $ fL : num [1:50, 1:50] 1 0.677 0.692 0.674 0.684 ... head(st1$hybrids, 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| hybrid| line_A| line_B| trait1| trait2| trait3| |------:|------:|------:|----------:|----------:|---------:| | 1| 1| 26| -0.6880637| 0.1907069| 0.0153955| | 2| 2| 26| -0.6102738| -0.0320787| 1.4661012| | 3| 3| 26| -0.3094099| -0.5013539| 0.2137806|
::: ::: For real data the same function is called with your own matrices: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} st1 <- stage1_build( X = hybrid_markers, # N x m, coded 0/1/2 or 0/0.5/1 ped = pedigree, # data.frame with columns a, b traits = predicted_traits, # N x n_traits fL = line_coancestry, # optional coding = "012" # or "0-0.5-1"; NULL (default) auto-detects ) ``` ::: `stage1_build()` rescales 0/1/2 dosages to 0/0.5/1 before computing `f`. With `coding = NULL` it infers the coding from the values present, ignoring missing calls: any value above 1 means 0/1/2. That rule assumes a 0/1/2 matrix contains at least one dosage-2 call. A matrix holding only 0 and 1 is ambiguous -- inbred lines coded 0/0.5/1, or 0/1/2 dosages with no homozygote for the allele coded 2 -- and no rule applied to the values can resolve it; `stage1_build()` then assumes 0/0.5/1 and warns. Declaring `coding` removes the assumption. On the simulated hybrids, which contain dosage-2 calls, the two codings give the same `f`: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} tr <- st1$hybrids[, grep("^trait", names(st1$hybrids))] pd <- data.frame(a = st1$hybrids$line_A, b = st1$hybrids$line_B) stopifnot(any(st1$X * 2 == 2), identical(stage1_build(st1$X, pd, tr)$f, stage1_build(st1$X * 2, pd, tr)$f)) ``` ::: The ambiguous case: two hybrids at three markers, coded 0/1/2, with no dosage-2 call. Auto-detection reads each 1 as a homozygote, so it returns the coancestry of two inbred individuals that these hybrids are not; the declared coding returns the coancestry computed directly from the 0/0.5/1 matrix (@tbl-coding-ambiguous). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} X_amb <- rbind(c(0, 1, 1), c(1, 0, 1)) # 0/1/2 dosages, no dosage 2 ped_amb <- data.frame(a = 1:2, b = 3:4) tr_amb <- data.frame(trait1 = c(0, 0)) f_auto <- withCallingHandlers( stage1_build(X_amb, ped_amb, tr_amb)$f, warning = function(w) { message("warning: ", conditionMessage(w)) invokeRestart("muffleWarning") }) f_012 <- stage1_build(X_amb, ped_amb, tr_amb, coding = "012")$f f_true <- molecular_coancestry(X_amb / 2) stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(f_012, f_true)), !isTRUE(all.equal(f_auto, f_true))) ``` ::: ::: {#tbl-coding-ambiguous .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Molecular coancestry of the two hybrids of the ambiguous example (`f11`, `f22`: self-coancestries; `f12`: between them) as returned by `stage1_build()` with the coding auto-detected and with `coding = "012"` declared, and as computed directly by `molecular_coancestry()` on the matrix divided by 2.'} ```{.r .cell-code} fmt(data.frame( coding = c("auto-detected", "declared 012", "direct, X / 2"), f11 = c(f_auto[1, 1], f_012[1, 1], f_true[1, 1]), f22 = c(f_auto[2, 2], f_012[2, 2], f_true[2, 2]), f12 = c(f_auto[1, 2], f_012[1, 2], f_true[1, 2]))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|coding | f11| f22| f12| |:-------------|------:|------:|------:| |auto-detected | 1.0000| 1.0000| 0.3333| |declared 012 | 0.6667| 0.6667| 0.5000| |direct, X / 2 | 0.6667| 0.6667| 0.5000|
::: ::: ## What the candidate pool looks like @fig-candidate-pool shows the two quantities every later chapter trades: the index of the candidates and the gene diversity of random subsets of them. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.2, 4.2, 2.5, 1)) hist(ctx$index, breaks = 40, col = "grey85", border = "white", main = "multi-trait index", xlab = "index (s.d. units)") n_sub <- 60 # random-subset size, a typical n_sel set.seed(cfg$seed + 3) gd_random <- replicate(400, gene_diversity(sample.int(ctx$N, n_sub), ctx)) hist(gd_random, breaks = 30, col = "grey85", border = "white", main = paste("GD of random subsets of", n_sub), xlab = "gene diversity") abline(v = gene_diversity(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx), col = book_pal[["ink"]], lwd = 2) par(op) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The candidate pool at the book scale (25 + 25 lines, 625 A x B hybrids, 2000 markers). Left: histogram of the multi-trait selection index of the 625 hybrids: the equally weighted sum of the standardised predicted traits (default `weights` of `build_ctx()`), re-standardised to mean 0 and s.d. 1. Right: histogram of the gene diversity of 400 random subsets of 60 hybrids, the baseline every later chapter measures against; dark vertical line: gene diversity of the whole candidate pool.](03-simulating-crosses_files/figure-html/fig-candidate-pool-1.png){#fig-candidate-pool fig-align='center' fig-alt='Two histograms. Left: the multi-trait index of the 625 candidate hybrids. Right: gene diversity of 400 random 60-hybrid subsets, with a dark vertical line for the whole pool lying to the right of the bulk of the distribution' width=1050} ::: ::: The dark vertical line is the gene diversity of the *whole* pool. It does not sit at the centre of the distribution of random subsets of 60 -- it sits above it. That gap is pure sampling, it has nothing to do with selection, and mistaking it for a loss is the subject of @sec-baseline. @tbl-gd-baseline gives the size of the gap. ::: {#tbl-gd-baseline .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Gene diversity of the whole candidate pool, mean gene diversity of the random subsets of @fig-candidate-pool, and the apparent loss: their difference as a percentage of the whole-pool value.'} ```{.r .cell-code} stopifnot(gene_diversity(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx) > mean(gd_random)) fmt(data.frame( quantity = c("GD, whole pool", "GD, mean of random subsets", "apparent loss (%)"), value = c(gene_diversity(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx), mean(gd_random), 100 * (gene_diversity(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx) - mean(gd_random)) / gene_diversity(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx)))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
